title: Notes of Ministry - 72 - November 1978

paragraphs.text: It is a blessed thing to speak a word to the saints, but a very solemn thing; it is a blessed thing to have to do with God, but a solemn thing too. We have been enjoying together the blessedness of being in that divine sphere and the circle of divine relationships. I want to speak a brief word, with the Spirit’s help, on experience with God; for how we come into the enjoyment and the possession of things is through experience. Divine resources are all there that we might enjoy the inheritance, but it has to be taken up by way of experience, experience with the blessed Trinity; the Father’s love and grace; the love and grace of our Lord Jesus, and of the Holy Spirit. Even if you are growing old and you feel weak in body, the Priest is there available to help you in relation to the things of God.

Now just a brief word on these two great men, great men in God’s eyes and undertakings in the Old Testament—Jacob, and Abraham the friend of God, and their experience, how they came into things by having direct experience with God. Our brother said yesterday that there is no substitute for experience, for the time you spend with the Lord. There is no substitute for the time you spend with divine Persons. We may read and acquire certain knowledge and light—what a lot we owe to the great ministries that have gone before; I suppose that nearly all we have we have acquired from

others. But then it has to be made good in your soul, and I think divine Persons are longing that we might have more intimate experience with them daily, individually; it would bring wealth and richness into our experience assemblywise. For the assembly is normally made up, surely, of persons who are overcomers, persons who have had to do with God, persons who are judging themselves, who are imbibing and deriving from Christ the living Head. All this brings substance into our souls.

It was a critical time, a crucial time, for Jacob; what an experience! He left his wives and his cattle, left his belongings—he was alone with God. It was an all-night matter. How real it was to Jacob; but he was determined with spiritual tenacity to get the blessing, and that is commendable, beloved brethren, to heaven, a brother or sister who is determined to get the blessing. Spiritual tenacity marked Jacob even though the Lord might be raising an issue with him and weakening him on the natural line, touching the sinew, the strength of Jacob. He had been crooked, like many of us, but here the Lord in discipline was having to do with him and weakened him. But you see Jacob would not let Him go, would not let Him go without the blessing. Is that not fine? We want to be more serious and definite about our relations with the Lord and with God. Do not be put off by the devil; do not be put off by anybody; make time. I understand Mr. Taylor loved that hymn, ‘Take time to be holy’. Take time to be with the Lord, take time to get through to God, because you will have opposition—not opposition from divine Persons; the struggle in Ephesians 6 is not with God, you know, the struggle is with the devil, with spiritual wickedness in heavenly places; we wrestle not with blood and flesh but with spiritual wickedness in heavenly places.

So the devil is against us, against young people, against every one of us; he wants the young people for the world, not for Christ. We have got to overcome the devil, we have got to resist him and say, ‘No, I am going to be for the Lord; I am going to get alone in my bedroom with the Lord and speak to Him’. You can always speak to divine Persons; at any time night or day you can speak to Them; They are always ready to hear, as though you were the only person on the earth. God takes, an interest in you as though you are the only one He is interested in, and He is doing that to thousands and myriads. He is so great He can give you His personal attention. God gave His personal attention here to Jacob, and Jacob went through and prevailed. He wrestled, he got the blessing, and he became a prince. What an experience! Would it not be worth it, a night of wrestling, if you became princely? If you put off the Jacob feature, if you put off the old man with his deeds, if you put off self and selfishness and put on the new man, if you put on what is spiritual and what is new, is it not worth the wrestling? Is it not worth the discipline? We are all in the school of God; we are all undergoing the Father’s discipline if we are sons. What is the end of it? That we may be partakers of the Father’s holiness.

So I want to draw the attention of the beloved brethren to this experience, crucial as it was and crippling on the natural line; he became a cripple, but what spirituality he gained! And it says that he saw God. God was not revealed as He is today in christianity, but Jacob says, “I have seen God face to face”. What an experience, what intimacy! As far as God was revealed he saw God face to face, not as we would see Him in the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but he had to do with God in an intimate way and his life was preserved. Wonderful! that is the gospel, is it not, how we as sinners can have to do with a holy God and not be condemned but be saved. That is Romans, how God can be just and justify him that is of the faith of Jesus (see Romans 3: 26).
Now the sun rose upon him, just as if it rose upon no one else, suggesting divine approval.

Beloved brethren, would we not seek, we who are older, to finish our days with divine approval? The sun rose upon him; God was pleased with him. Now Jacob has come to be princely, come to appreciate the spiritual as over against the natural, the spiritual as over against the carnal, his scheming and his own will; he has come to prove that God can do the very best for him, far better than he could do for himself. His will is the best. So the warm rays of the sun rose upon him as he had a sense of divine approval and divine favour. What an experience! May it be ours, beloved. May we know something of what it is to wrestle in secret; there is a lot to wrestle for. There are assembly matters for concern; we need to see the principles involved in them and be one about principles, and when we are one about principles perhaps God will come in for us and bring a solution. We want to see what the enemy is at, what is at stake. The enemy has a certain design, and we want to see through all that may be on the surface and see what the devil is at. So that while Jacob was a limping man he was a spiritual man, he became a spiritual man through experience with God personally. It is to be coveted, beloved.

Now I want to draw attention to Abraham’s experience. God raises this matter of circumcision in chapter 17. He insists on it, in fact it says in Genesis 17: 22, “And he left off talking with him; and God went up from Abraham”, as much as to say, ‘I

have left the matter with you, Abraham; I am not deviating from this. I am not allowing the flesh in any shape or form. Ishmael may be your son naturally but I am not having to do with the flesh or countenancing or supporting that at all; you must come to my judgment about the flesh. Think about it; think it over’. And Abraham came to it; thank God he came to it, that he must be circumcised and all in his house. He comes into line, in our language, with the cross of Christ where the flesh has been entirely cut off, particularly as it is presented in Colossians, “the putting off of the body of the flesh, in the circumcision of the Christ”

(Colossians 2: 11). So if God has finished with the flesh, finished with that order of man in the cross of Christ, if it cost Him so much to give His Son up to end that kind of man, we must come to it ourselves. The moral meaning of circumcision would be that we have a judgment of the flesh.

Now Abraham had that judgment. All who were born in his house or bought with money were circumcised, so that he is in a good state of soul now for an experience with God, and what a choice experience he had. There he was sitting at the tent-door in the heat of the day.

When he might have been resting he was spiritually alert and restful at the tent-door, ready for a divine appearing. I believe we need the state of soul for a divine appearing. If we are going on in a careless, indifferent, or earthly way, and minding things that we should not, perhaps divine Persons will not draw near to us. But Abraham, a circumcised man, is ready now for this divine appearing. Jehovah appeared to him by the oaks of Mamre. He is in line with the purpose of God, sitting by the tent-door in the heat of the day. “And he lifted up his eyes and saw, and behold, three men standing near him”. Is there a veiled

allusion to the Trinity there? Was not God longing to reveal Himself as Father, Son and Holy Spirit; though the fulness of time had not yet come for the revelation of God in the fulness of His name? But Abraham is such a friend of God that it is as if He gives this veiled allusion and they stationed themselves so that Abraham could avail himself of them. Very fine that, is it not? “And he lifted up his eyes and saw, and behold, three men standing near him. And when he saw them, he ran to meet them”.

He was alert, he was in exercise, he wanted an experience with God. May we long for an experience with God daily, and in assembly matters too. May we not be content until we reach consciously in assembly service the fulness of God. Blessed indeed it is to respond to the Father, but as we proceed the Father would strengthen us by His Spirit that we may go inward into the blessedness of the fulness of God, God all in all, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and realise the end of the purpose and ways of God. It is a blessed experience to worship the Fulness. Abraham ran to meet them, “he ran to meet them from the tent-door, and bowed himself to the earth”. Is that not beautiful? What a reverent state with him! “Lord, if now I have found favour in thine eyes …”—Why did he not say ‘lords’? It was spiritual intuition; he was a spiritual man. Where had he got it? By intimacy and communion with God; that is where we grow, that is where we get spiritual intuition. He said, “Lord”, he recognised that God was there. “If now I have found favour in thine eyes”—see the spirit of humility—“pass not away, I pray thee, from thy servant. Let now a little water be fetched, that ye may wash your feet, and rest yourselves under the tree. And I will fetch a morsel of bread; and refresh yourselves; after
that ye shall pass on; for therefore have ye passed on towards your servant. And they said, So do as thou hast said”. They were ready to be detained by Abraham.
Think of being able to detain the Lord, to detain divine Persons! Mary was such in John 11

and 12, a spiritual person who could detain the Lord and influence Him, for when Jesus saw Mary weeping, and the Jews weeping. He was “deeply moved in spirit”. A spiritual person can detain the Lord; Oh how choice it is! It involves experience with the Lord, experience with the Spirit, experience with the Father. It will be our eternal portion, beloved, in eternal conditions with bodies of glory to enjoy the revelation of God in that blessed Man. It will be experience with God, and experience with the saints too, intercourse with the saints in heaven. It makes you really long for that experience.
So Abraham was able to detain Jehovah; “So do as thou hast said”. What an experience! May experience with God be ours increasingly, beloved, for His name’s sake.

I was thinking, dear brethren, of this manifestation and the gain of it. It is interesting how John, by the Spirit of course, so many years after they occurred, recalls these manifestations and the way the Lord was manifested

each time. It raises the question with us as to whether we can recall what happened even last Lord’s day. John says, “And he manifested himself thus”. Well, how did the Lord manifest Himself last to the saints in Birmingham or in Malvern? With John the manifestation is distinct and he gives us the impression that the Lord is very ready to manifest Himself; he says it “is already the third time”. Whether it was week by week we do not know, but the Lord did manifest Himself the third time although, dear brethren, they had all gone a little astray.

I think we have to allow—I suggest it and I would submit it for the brethren’s judgment—for the Lord’s sovereignty in manifestation, because this third time they had all come under a lead, or an influence, that was not what it should have been. They not only came under the influence of it but they said, ‘We will go too’. I do not think that is unknown in our experience. Still, the Lord manifested Himself to them and it does seem to me, beloved, that we should not have too much difficulty, on the basis of this scripture, as to whether the Lord did manifest Himself to us in a past decade. At one of the previous manifestations at least one of the twelve was missing, and John recalls these facts and they are recalled for us by the Spirit for our teaching. Each one was distinct; you can hardly think of the Lord coming in in exactly the same manner and leaving exactly the same impression. There is no lack with Him; there is an abundance, beloved, of what He would convey to us, impressions of His glory, of some particular aspect of His work, some particular facet of what He is to the Father maybe, what He is as the Firstborn among many brethren. I would like to be able to say more definitely, ‘He manifested Himself thus’.
But He came; how long it was between the
second and third we do not know but it was long enough for Peter to feel again the pull of the sea. That is a well known thing of course. A poet wrote some lines on ‘Sea Fever’—
‘I must down to the seas again, to
the lonely sea and the sky,
And all I ask is a tall ship and a star
to steer her by’.

We have all got a ‘pull’ beloved, and we should face it and we should identify it and discover whether it is pulling us in the right direction; whether it is pulling us closer to Christ and to His things or whether it is pulling us away. It may be legitimate, it may be something that in measure we have to fill out, but we have to watch any influence that may pull us away from what is really our chief interest. Beloved, let it be so, our chief interest. Did not the psalmist speak about that (see Psalm 137: 6)?

Well, Peter did succumb, but he did not succumb again after this, I think. The Lord manifested Himself the third time and subsequently He went on high and Peter and the others remained at Jerusalem. For ten whole days Peter stayed there. I think it might be right to say that this third manifestation had the effect of settling Peter. It says, “where were staying”

(Acts 1: 13); in that upper room they stayed. The Lord did not come, the Spirit had not come, and for ten days they waited. I love to think of this, beloved. Peter in Jerusalem, landlocked, and for those ten days he withstood the pull of the sea. He stayed in the upper room, and I would suggest that he had got the benefit of the Lord’s manifesting Himself the third time.
So a manifestation is to have an effect on us, a permanent and abiding effect. I am not saying it is not also to have a special effect on the week; I think it is; I think one would see that If one

were more ready to discern it. The Lord would give a pointer; the way He manifests Himself would be a pointer for the week because He sees ahead, even if we do not; but it is also to have an abiding effect. So that the next time He comes we are, so to speak, more in tune, more ready, more in spiritual form, more alert to discern Him and say, ‘Yes, it was certainly thus that He came’. One feels how nebulous one can be. ‘Yes, we had a good impression’.
What was it? We have to stop and think. ‘He manifested Himself thus’! May we be helped to get clear and definite and distinct impressions as the Lord comes amongst us, for His name’s sake.
One has been carrying the thought in the week since the occasion of the Supper of how
‘The bride, with Thee in nearness,
Adds lustre to the scene’. (Hymn 352)

God is sufficient in Himself, needing no addition, but immediately you admit the incarnation you allow for the great matter of addition. I wish to say a word about how the great matter of suffering will influence and modify the rule in the world to come. I trust what I have to say will not be altogether out of accord with the tenor of these meetings. I thought I got a bit of confirmation yesterday when the pearl was referred to. All sorts of precious stones are in the foundation of the wall of the heavenly city, but when you come to the gates you come to the pearl. A pearl is something worked out to a result by a living creature in circumstances

of irritation and suffering. You could not say that about other precious stones. It may be that the pearl gives the idea of lustre more than any of the other precious stones. It is a wonderful suggestion, the lustre of it. You think, beloved brethren, what kind of rule it will be, so beneficent as the great Ruler and His consort are there.

So I just offer a few words on the great matter of suffering that will contribute to the kind of rule in that day. For, after all, she is the Lamb’s wife as well as the bride, and it is principally the Lamb’s wife that I wish to bring forward. In that wonderful scene of perfection of light she is a great vessel of light; but you think of everything coming through those gates, each gate respectively of one pearl. It is pronounced; the idea of one pearl pervades throughout the city; it is bound to influence the kind of rule. There is a good deal of suffering, beloved brethren, sufferings of many kinds. You could not conceive that these sufferings will not work out to some result in the whole matter of the pearl. Where is the family, where is the household, where is the person that is not going through sufferings that maybe few know about? I even venture to think as to what comes on us maybe as the result of our own doing that even from that, if in self-judgment we get before the Lord, there will be that which will contribute to this great matter of the Lamb’s wife. I could not think of the Lord, loving us so much, not bringing something out of whatever may come upon us in the way of suffering.

So 2 Corinthians 4 stands out—“Our momentary and light affliction works for us in surpassing measure an eternal weight of glory”. There are two lines which run through Scripture. In our brother’s reference to Jacob you see these two lines in one man, Jacob and Israel, Jacob representing the moral

line, the line of experience with God, Israel the princely line, the side of the anointing. The one line has its part in the testimony, the other shines more in the service of God, the one bearing on the other no doubt. I think these two lines run through Scripture, seen in the brass and the gold. Brass is the moral side of things, where things are worked out in experience with God, and it is this line that I wish to speak about. It goes right through. Smyrna, along with Philadelphia, is the church against which the Lord has nothing, but Smyrna brings up the side of brass, the moral line running into the Lamb’s wife. The other line runs down through the gold into Philadelphia, into the bride. These are the two lines that God is working out, and He works everything out to a complete result; in both lines He has His perfect accomplishment.

2 Corinthians 4 brings up the great matter of suffering. Beloved brethren, may we be comforted, as Paul says in another place, “For I reckon that the sufferings of this present time are not worthy to be compared with the coming glory to be revealed to us”, Romans 8: 18.

May we be comforted by these things that, whatever the suffering, there is something to be wrought out. And in this wonderful chapter, with all the pressure of things, twice over you get “we faint not”; it is mercy being poured in, you might say, while He is working out His great thoughts in regard of this vessel, the vessel He is producing in view of the world to come. Let us not be circumscribed in our thoughts but let us take the long view; I think faith does that, faith looks on ahead, it looks on to the coming glory. May we be comforted therefore in the face of whatever the sufferings may be. You think of the mental anguish, the mortification too, that is with you sometimes; the awful breakdown in the

testimony, the shambles that you may have made of things; families disrupted, and then too the physical suffering that the saints endure—the quota from each of these sufferings will go into the Lamb’s wife. You can be sure about that.

I want to refer to a type. Solomon made the vessels of gold himself it would seem; that is what the Lord does by a heavenly ministry; Ephesians 4 is the scripture for that, what the Lord brings about by way of formation by a heavenly ministry. But the vessels of brass for the temple were made by Hiram; he was an expert in the working of brass and it says he made all those vessels, he cast them in the clay-ground near the Jordan (see 1 Kings 7: 46).

That is very significant. The Lord brings His people into the area of death, right within the region of death—maybe specially in physical sufferings—but, beloved brethren, He works out His thoughts, they are cast in the clay-ground. 2 Corinthians 4 brings up the clay-ground, our mortal flesh, the outward man; that is all in the area of the clay-ground; but He is working out His thoughts.

The molten metal was cast into these moulds, and in moulding you dare not touch the cast until it is set. You wonder sometimes; you are called to go through a set of sufferings and there is no let-up; there does not seem to be any way out. Hiram would tell you, ‘I dare not touch the cast until it is set; the whole thing would be spoiled if I interfered with the cast until it is really set’. In 2 Corinthians 4 where you get this kind of thing in teaching, as I said, the Lord all the time is supplying mercy for us. He gives His present supply of mercy to support us and to sustain us that we might not faint under His hand. Well, He is working out something in view of His own service that is bound to come into evidence, as I said, to
influence and modify the rule in the day to come. May we be comforted by these thoughts.

I have in mind to say a little, dear brethren, as to what is distinctive, and, of course, the mind immediately goes to Christ, the Lord Jesus. Unique and incomparable, He stands out alone as God’s ideal. One feels very inadequate in seeking to speak of this great matter, for who can compass the greatness of Christ? Our apprehension of Him is at best feeble but, thank God, it is there. Thank God for the appreciation of Christ that there is in the hearts of His saints! The time was when there was no beauty in Him that we should desire Him. That is the flesh, which is not only incapable of appreciating His glories but indeed despises Him. He is not a Man that we would naturally appreciate but is the One upon whom God could open the heavens to announce, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I have found my delight”, Matthew 17: 5. What a Man is Jesus! He will engage our hearts eternally. How the heart wells forth in the contemplation of Christ! What a need there is, dear brethren, especially for those of us who are younger, to find time to contemplate the blessedness of Christ, His unique humanity, His work, His many glories. Unless we have some impression of the greatness and glory of Christ we shall not stand in these difficult days.

I should like to impress our hearts with the greatness of Christ in His distinctiveness, the red heifer being a wonderful type of the Lord Jesus. There are many types in the Old Testament which bring out the glory of Christ, but there is something here which is very beautiful and distinctive. What is red is normally associated in scripture with what is distinctive, which led me to this scripture—“Speak unto the children of Israel, that they bring thee a red heifer without blemish, wherein is no defect, and upon which never came yoke”. There was only one Man of whom this could be said. Think of the holy perfections of Christ. Think of the manhood that could be tested and tried. The enemy tested Him with everything that was within his power, the Lord allowing Himself to be tested. What grace was in that, dear brethren—the Man who is Himself over all, God blessed for ever, allowing Himself to be tested by Satan. There was not an element in the Lord that could fail to answer to the test. He said, “The ruler of the world comes, and in me he has nothing”, John 14: 30.
Then it says, “Ye shall give it to Eleazar the priest, and he shall bring it outside the camp, and one shall slaughter it before him”. What impresses me is, ‘one shall slaughter it before him’.

It goes on to say in verse 5, ‘And one shall burn the heifer before his eyes’. I think it implies that the Spirit would keep the death of Christ freshly before us. Eleazar would have had to witness this. You will remember that when the Lord was in Gethsemane He chose three disciples to be with Him. Think of the untold agonies of the Lord Jesus as He contemplated the sufferings of the cross. His sweat falling to the earth as great drops of blood. Think of these three men who were chosen to take account of that. The Lord was withdrawn from them about a stone’s throw; they could go so far, but
there came a point where the Lord had to go the whole way alone. How affecting it is! As the hymn says—
‘None could follow there, blest Saviour’ (Hymn 298)
I think the Holy Spirit would bring all this up to date in each of our hearts, that we should contemplate the glory of the humanity of Christ, the way He went, His sufferings. It says,

“And one shall burn the heifer before his eyes; its skin and its flesh, and its blood, with its dung, shall he burn”. I would like just to leave an impression of the completeness of what Christ did on the cross so that we should be cleansed from every defiling element.

After that it says, “And the priest shall take”—this is something the priest has to do—“cedar-wood, and hyssop, and scarlet, and cast them into the midst of the burning …”. As we allow the Spirit of God to impress us with the greatness of what Christ has done in removing every vestige of the first order of man as before God, we find that we can cast these things in. It means that we come to God’s judgment in regard to the first order. These things speak of man in the flesh; the cedar-wood is the pride of man; the scarlet is what would distinguish man.

We all like to be distinguished by something, do we not? Naturally none of us likes to be put completely out of sight; we all like to hold on to something, even the hyssop, fleshly humility. How difficult it may be to cast in the hyssop! You think of the features of man in the world which would make him stand out. In the light of the cross of Christ everything has to go.

As we take account of those words that came from the lips of the Lord Jesus, “My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?” (Psalm 22: 1)—who can give an answer to that? Thank God, the believer can give an answer—“And thou art holy, thou that

dwellest amid the praises of Israel”. Thank God, the believer, by the Spirit, is intelligent as to the way that Christ has had to go. Christendom seeks to attach the Lord’s name to many things that are abhorrent to God, to a vast system where all these things that mark man are seen in their supposed glory, but the cedar-wood, the hyssop, and the scarlet have all to go. O, dear brethren, how difficult it is to relinquish what belongs to these! But then if we go through the exercises of Romans the believer comes to it—“But if, by the Spirit, ye put to death ...” (Romans 8: 13)—there you are using a divine Person, speaking reverently, to have done with these things that belong to the first order. Then what is the result? You come through to life. Life in yourself? No, life in another Man! Oh there is liberty and freedom in coming through to this kind of life, the life that is in Christ Jesus.

Well, God has that in view for every one of us. You know, there is nothing in this life really to bring in lasting happiness and liberty, but when you get through to the life that is in Christ Jesus you come through to a great sphere where everything is vibrant with life, where there is joy and peace; “For the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness, and peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit”, Romans.14: 17. It is all in the range of the Holy Spirit.
These are wonderful things. Dear young ones, I would address myself to you especially, commit yourselves to this. You will prove that what I am saying is the truth.

I read in Timothy because here we have a young man being addressed. This speaks of the time when Paul’s ministry had been set aside, when the church publicly was in breakdown and ruins, but here is a young man to whom Paul addresses himself; not a

young man of renown or great personality—he would very likely be timid and was obviously not a strong man physically. He was one that very likely you would not pick out in a crowd, but that is the kind of young man in whom God is going to bring out this great feature of what is distinctive. I do not mean in the sense of making a great impact in the world, but I speak—

about distinction as God views it, something that is delightful to Him. You think of a world in which men are going their own way; there is a whole list of things at the beginning of this chapter—“difficult times shall be there; for men shall be lovers of self, lovers of money, boastful, arrogant, evil speakers” (2 Timothy 3: 2). In the world these things are seen more and more every day. What it is for God to have a young man who can go against the stream, who can stand out—and I could use the phrase ‘in moral glory’, for I have no doubt that there is a moral glory in it; not that it is to attract any glory to ourselves, but it attaches glory to the One who can make a man stand and be designated “man of God”.

So the word “thou” in verse 10 is emphatic, bringing out the point that there is something there that stands out in the scene where everything is so obnoxious to God—“Thou hast been thoroughly acquainted with my teaching, conduct, purpose, faith, longsuffering, love, endurance, persecutions, sufferings—what sufferings happened to me in Antioch, in Iconium, in Lystra”. This young man was acquainted with the testimony and the way in which it had been brought through in power. You dear young ones, I would urge you to acquaint yourselves with the course of the testimony because you will find in doing so that God is supporting a line of things that He is going to bring through and maintain for His own glory eternally.
I was struck in reading about Abigail. She was acquainted with the testimony. She acquainted

herself with the acts of David. She was attached to a churlish man, Nabal. That is the position in which we are, attached publicly to something that has brought great dishonour on the Lord’s name. This is something from which we cannot escape. Abigail was married to Nabal; in one sense it was something that she could not avoid; but then she had a knowledge of David and she could speak of him as one who had enemies, but Jehovah was supporting him.
That is what I would impress upon us. Take account of the testimony and you will find that there is a line that the Lord is supporting. Commit yourselves to that. It brings in suffering.

Paul says, “All indeed who desire to live piously in Christ Jesus will be persecuted. But wicked men and juggling imposters shall advance in evil” (2 Timothy 3: 12, 13). If we looked at that naturally it would bring in despondency, because what is wicked and evil apparently has the ascendancy; the whole world lies in the wicked one. But Paul is encouraging this young man and he says, “But thou, abide in those things which thou hast learned, and of which thou hast been fully persuaded”.

I would like to pass on this encouragement. If you have been brought up in an area where Paul’s ministry is held dear, thank God for that. I would just put it to you—“Abide in those things which thou hast learned … knowing of whom thou hast learned them; and that from a child thou hast known the sacred letters, which are able to make thee wise unto salvation, through faith which is in Christ Jesus”. What a sphere to come into; what a sphere of salvation! The Spirit will give you wisdom and He will give you power; He will give you understanding. That is the feature that marked Abigail—she was a woman of discernment, a woman of understanding. Paul says earlier in this epistle, “God has not given us a spirit of

cowardice, but of power, and of love, and of wise discretion” (1 Timothy 1: 7). God would fit us for the testimony. A spirit of power would make you stand in relation to all that is adverse so that you can find your way as led by the Spirit of God. God is able to maintain you in the pathway of His will in a sphere where there is so much against you.

Then Paul says, “Every scripture is divinely inspired, and profitable for teaching, for conviction, for correction, for instruction in righteousness; that the man of God may be complete, fully fitted to every good work”. The footnote says this involves being ‘complete as to qualifications’. God being who He is, He requires something distinctive to represent Him here; not the kind of qualifications that Christendom has taken up—a university degree, a knowledge of theology; all that kind of thing is valueless in the sight of God. He takes account of a man who in lowliness and humility commits himself to what is here that is of the Lord Jesus. God will help such a man—young man, it may be. God will take account of you and He will help you to stand. He will help you to be here as a man of God. I think that is a beautiful description; I think it is one of the greatest things that could be said of any man that he can be described as a ‘man of God’. At the beginning God said, “Let us make man”

(Genesis 1: 26); you think of God setting up man, the perfection that was there in Adam. Sin has come in, causing degradation and distance, but God, by the Holy Spirit, can rescue a man and support him, take him away from the whole system of things that is around and make him stand so as to represent Him rightly. Think of a young man in his office, or a young person at school, feeling weak but relying on the help of the Holy Spirit to represent God.

These are great things, dear brethren; I would I knew more of them by experience, but may every one of us take account of these things, take account of what is for us. It is a great thing to be aware that the Spirit of God is for us. Then you think of Christ on high sanctifying Himself in regard to His people; “I sanctify myself for them”. He says, John 17: 19. The Lord Jesus has set Himself apart in order to serve His people. So we have the priestly love and intercession of Christ, the power of the Holy Spirit down here, and the Father’s love and care and compassion. From the divine side there is nothing lacking; it only involves, dear brethren, that we lay hold on these things, that we take account firstly of Christ and His greatness and moral perfection as the great object and pattern, and then by the Holy Spirit are helped to be conformed to that.

May the Lord help us in these things. They are very great, and I suppose we all feel that we come far short, but the great thing is to strive earnestly. Lay hold on these things, and ask the Spirit to help you. Thus we shall all be helped together and will go on together in the great things of God. May the Lord help us in it for His name’s sake.
Lord Jesus Christ Thy lovers far and near
All call for Thee.
We long to see Thy face and hear Thy shout
Of victory,
To see Thee as Thou art in glory bright,
The assembly with Thee for Thine own delight.
The universe will then respond with joy
And liberty,
And all with breath will find their blest employ
In praising Thee;
Ten thousand thousand voices join as one
And by Thee rise to worship God alone.
Help us then, Lord, with Thee e’en now to be
With single eye,
‘Midst deep’ning darkness serve Thee faithfully
Where Thou didst die,
Thy suffering love to which we owe our all
Binding together those who on Thee call.
Melbourne, 1977
PERFECTION When God begins a work He has in view, and will reach, a perfect result.

David had the sense of this in Psalm 138—“Though I walk in the midst of trouble, thou wilt revive me … Jehovah will perfect what concerneth me”. How comforting to have this assurance, that even trouble and adversity are being used to bring about what is perfect. In the parable as to the sower the Lord likens the seed that fell among thorns to those who “bring no fruit to perfection” (Luke 8: 14), showing that perfect fruit was in His mind, the work of God reaching a full, rich result. This can only be by the Spirit. Paul says to the Galatians, “Having begun in Spirit, are ye going to be made perfect in flesh?”. The legal line among them sought to recognise the flesh, but if there is to be a perfect result for God it must be “in Spirit”.

So let us have perfection before us. Even to the young company at Thessalonica Paul speaks of perfection—“night and day beseeching exceedingly to the end that we may see your face, and perfect what is lacking in your faith”, 1 Thessalonians 3: 10. Paul’s steady aim in his toil and combat was to “present every man perfect in Christ”, Colossians l: 28.
Then God is working to secure perfection in the assembly, spoken of typically in Psalm 50 as “Zion, the perfection of beauty”. What a rich field for meditation there is in that expression!

God will reach His end. Wherever His eye rests there will be perfect beauty in formation according to Christ, in intelligence, grace, adornment, a beauty the like of which has never before been seen, fully answering to the ideals of eternal pleasure and purpose. It will shine under the divine gaze for the delight and glory and rest of God. Already in the service of God we have a powerful sense of it.

So perfection is to be before us in our prayers and in our service. If in any measure we are God’s fellow-workmen then we must have His own great objectives before us, and along with that a keen and sensitive judgment of every element that would interfere with progress toward them.
